what_it_does: Processors speed up memory access by predicting which data you will need next and fetching it early into a small, fast cache — a technique called prefetching. The processor uses virtual memory addresses (the labels it sees) before the hardware translates them to real physical locations. A tricky edge case arises when a predicted address crosses a page boundary (a page being the basic unit of virtual memory mapping): sometimes those cross-page prefetches are helpful, sometimes harmful, and it depends on the workload and even the moment in execution. MOKA is a design framework for building a small filter circuit that sits alongside an existing prefetcher and decides, prediction by prediction, whether to allow or block page-crossing requests. It uses lightweight learned predictors (similar in spirit to branch predictors — small tables that learn patterns from program behavior) combined with real-time awareness of how busy the address-translation hardware and memory-request buffers are. The result is instantiated as a prototype called DRIPPER that plugs into three well-known prefetcher designs without modifying them.
